_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Well? Did Hap get off the ground, and did Ole get his hay in dry?

replies.say: Both. Hap at ten sharp, and Ole sent a pie.
replies.back: Two forecasts, two hits. Frame them before your luck changes. Rhubarb? Mrs. Haugen makes a rhubarb pie that could end a war. Save me a slice.

replies.say: Both. The goat ate my hat by way of thanks.
replies.back: That’s how the goat says thank you. It’s how it says most things.

turns.them: Good. Now, fresh troubles. Edna Pruitt telephoned me, long distance, if you please. The Ladies’ Aid picnic is Sunday afternoon, and if a lumpy grey sheet rolls in she wants to know whether to haul out the tent. She has a week’s washing to hang out, too. And Dutch Kessler at the elevator has three wagons of wheat sitting out under a grey sky that has been parked overhead for two days.

replies.say: Grey clouds mean rain, don’t they?
replies.back: Not always. Most grey clouds never drop a thing. That’s tonight’s lesson, as it happens.

replies.say: Why does she telephone you and not me?
replies.back: She’s known me twenty years and you two weeks. Win the picnic and you win the town.

turns.them: This week: why some days the air bubbles up and other days it lies flat, the lid that spreads heaps into a grey sheet, why most clouds never rain, and the one grey sky that always does. Then those questions answer themselves.

replies.say: Can I just tell everybody to carry an umbrella?
replies.back: You can. Then nobody will ever ask you anything again, and you can take up farming.

turns.them: One more. On a hot afternoon the air around gets colder by 12 degrees a kilometre as you go up. A thermal off Ole’s stubble field cools at 10. Does it keep rising?

replies.say: Yes. It stays warmer than the air around it.
replies.back: Right. It cools slower than its neighbours, so it keeps its lead and keeps on going. That’s an unstable day.

replies.say: No. It’s cooling, so it sinks.
replies.back: Everything that rises cools. What matters is whether it cools faster or slower than the air around it. Ten is slower than twelve, so it stays warmer and keeps going.

replies.say: Only if it makes a cloud.
replies.back: No cloud needed. Ten is slower than twelve, so it stays warmer than its neighbours and climbs all on its own.

turns.them: Hap says on days like that his airplane rides like a buckboard on a washboard road. Every one of those bumps is a bubble.

replies.back: And complaining about every one of them.

turns.them: So, a dark grey sheet overhead. Does dark mean rain?

replies.say: Not by itself. Depth matters more.
replies.back: Exactly. A thin sheet can look dark and give nothing but drizzle. It takes a deep cloud to grow drops heavy enough to fall.
That’s the knee talking. A thin sheet can look dark and never give more than drizzle. Depth makes rain, not darkness.
Only during picnics, Edna would say. No: depth makes rain, not darkness.

turns.them: Remember: a raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets’ worth of water. Most droplets never find enough friends.

replies.say: A million. That’s a lot of bumping.

turns.them: That’s the club’s photographs done. Now give Edna and Dutch their answers, and give them straight. Edna has two questions this week, the picnic and the washing, and she can smell a hedge at forty paces.

replies.say: Can I give Edna her answer in writing?
